ようこそ、ロサ エレナ — Welcome, Rosa Elena

You review the whole unit “N4 · Waiting”: what should be (～はず), what might be or surely is (～かもしれない / ～に ちがいない), what has been decided (～こと に する / なる), purpose and cause (～ため) and surprise (～のに) — on the day Rosa Elena is born.
Babies born exactly on their due date should be few.
And there I was, sure it would be born earlier.
Maybe it could hear my voice from inside the belly.

To review ～はず だ / はず が ない / はず だった and どうりで (ch. 41).
To review ～かもしれない, ～に ちがいない and the scale of certainty (ch. 42).
To review ～こと に する / こと に なる / こと に して いる / こと に なって いる (ch. 43).
To review ～ために (purpose and cause) and ～のに (ch. 44), and to choose correctly among all the forms of the unit.

15 January, afternoon, in a private room at the hospital where Mihai works. Rosa Elena was born this morning. Kenji comes to visit; Carmen is already there. Kenji and Carmen speak Spanish to each other, but here everything is given in Japanese.
(Opening the door quietly) …May I come in? I didn’t come for the ramen — I came to meet Hana-chan.
Kenji! Come in. She’s just woken up.
Wow… she’s so small. She really was born on the 15th.
Babies born right on the due date are supposed to be only about five percent.
(Laughing) Mum, your intuition missed again today.
At ten past five in the morning. A healthy little girl, three thousand two hundred grams.
He did cry. And right after she was born, he sang the lullaby.
Haruka’s lullaby? Even though you kept saying “I still sing it badly”?
Because I’d decided to sing it once Hana-chan was born. Even if I sang it badly, Hana-chan stopped crying straight away.
Maybe she could hear Mihai’s voice from inside the belly.
That must be it. After all, he sang every single evening.
Let me take a photo, so I can send it to Haruka and Sakura.
Go ahead. But everyone in Japan should have seen the photo by now. Mihai sent it this morning.
I see. No wonder Sakura called me so many times.
You said “call me anytime”, and yet last night you didn’t answer.
Then on the day you go home, we celebrate with Ramen Hana-chan. There should be thirty portions in the freezer.
…Actually, this morning Elena and I went home and the two of us ate three portions.
(Laughing) Twenty-seven portions, then. …Well, it’s a celebration, let’s call it fine.
“haitte mo ii?” = may I come in?
also; even; “~te mo ii” = it’s allowed
good; “ii koto ni shiyō” = let’s call it fine
“hazu da” = should; “kita hazu da” = no wonder
“umarete sugu” = right after birth; “umarete kara” = after being born
“koto ni shite ita” = I had decided; “koto ni naru” = it’s been decided; “koto ni shiyō” = let’s call it
ha-zu: the “u” is short, almost whispered. はずれる (ha-zu-re-ru) starts with the same two sounds — a handy memory trick: what “should” be (はず) sometimes misses (はずれる), like Carmen’s intuition.

chi-ga-i-na-i / ka-mo-shi-re-na-i: five and six short, even syllables respectively, linked, with no stress on any of them. In ちがいない the “i” in “ga-i” is pronounced clearly and separately: chi-ga-i, not a swallowed “chigai”.
san-zen (not “sansen”: after ん, せん becomes ぜん) ni-hya-ku gu-ra-mu. As in さんびゃく, ん changes the sound that follows.
はず is a LOGICAL deduction based on facts: a calendar, a statistic, something someone said. Mihai, as a doctor, knows the figures; Kenji knows he left 30 portions in the freezer.
was supposed to (but it didn’t happen)
Connections: verb / い-adj. in plain form + はず; な-adj. + な はず (しずか な はず); noun + の はず (やすみ の はず).
2. ～かもしれない and ～に ちがいない (ch. 42)
かもしれない = a possibility (about 50%); に ちがいない = a strong conviction, often from a feeling rather than from figures. Both attach directly to nouns and な-adjectives, WITHOUT だ: げんき かもしれない, げんき に ちがいない.
はやく うまれる に ちがいない。(Carmen)
Carmen “was sure” (に ちがいない) and got it wrong: に ちがいない shows how convinced you are, it guarantees nothing. That’s why Mihai the doctor prefers はず: it rests on figures.
3. ～こと に する / ～こと に なる (ch. 43)
it’s been decided (by others, by circumstances)
The discharge depends on the doctors and the hospital rules, not on Ana → こと に なりました. Kenji, who “forgives” the three eaten portions, makes the decision himself → こと に しよう.
Remember: after のに there is no request or suggestion (✗ あめ な のに、でかけましょう → ✓ あめ だ けど、でかけましょう). And な-adjectives / nouns need な: やすみ な のに.
5. Unit review: one birth, six ways to talk about it
The whole unit “N4 · Waiting” was about how to talk about something you don’t know for sure yet — and about what you do in the meantime. Here is the same birth, told with each tool:
She should be born on the 15th (so says the calendar).
She’s surely going to be born earlier (I can feel it).
We decided to name her Rosa Elena.
I made soup for the baby.
I thought she’d be born earlier, and yet she came right on time.

Culture: in Japan, the maternity ward usually gives parents the dried umbilical cord (へその お) in a small wooden box, kept for life as a keepsake. Friends send birth gifts (しゅっさん いわい), and the family replies with a small thank-you gift (うちいわい).

ひかり の なか で — In the light
On the evening of the 14th, Ana and her family ate fresh Ramen Hana-chan, made by Kenji.
“The due date is tomorrow, but she might not be born yet,” said Mihai.
Carmen said: “This child is surely coming out soon.” Even though she had said exactly the same thing at the false alarm.
When she had finished her ramen, Ana put down her chopsticks and placed a hand on her belly.
“…Mihai. This time it might be the real thing.”
Ana looked at the sheet stuck on the fridge: the “list for next time”, written after the false alarm.
Mihai looked at his jumper. This time it wasn’t inside out. Instead, he had one blue sock and one black one.
When he timed the gaps between the pains: ten minutes, ten minutes, nine. This time they were regular.
Cristina said on the phone: “Teacher, this time they must be real contractions. Go to the hospital.”
When they called Elena, they heard: “I’m coming right away! Don’t you forget me this time!”
They called Kenji too, but he didn’t answer. And he was the one who’d said “call me anytime”.
When they went out the door, Mrs Doina was standing on the stairs in her dressing gown. In her hand she was once again holding a thermos of hot tea.
“This time Rozița is surely coming! Good luck!” Upstairs, Mr Petre’s dog barked too, just once: “Woof!”
Mihai took Ana’s bag, took Ana by the hand, and they went slowly down the stairs.
The taxi came in ten minutes. When he saw the driver, Mihai was amazed: it was that old man with the white moustache.
“We meet again. It’s not snowing today, so this time we should get there faster.”
In front of the hospital, the old man again wouldn’t take the change. “This time for real — good luck, Mum!”
The doctor on duty was the same colleague of Mihai’s as on the night of the false alarm. “Today it’s the real thing. Don’t worry, everything is going to plan.”
The night was long. Mihai, even though he’s a doctor, couldn’t do anything: he just held Ana’s hand.
Ana would say something in Spanish, then cry out in Japanese “it hurts!”. Mihai kept repeating in Romanian: “You can do it!”
In the corridor, Elena and Carmen waited holding hands. Even though they had no language in common, they didn’t let go of each other’s hand even once.
And then, at ten past five in the morning, a strong first cry rang out in the room.
The tiny baby was crying on Ana’s chest.
Mihai couldn’t see anything for tears. Then he began to sing softly: Haruka’s lullaby.
It was the song he had decided to sing to her once she was born. He still sang it a bit badly.
But the baby stopped crying and opened her eyes a little.
“So she really could hear it from inside the belly,” Ana laughed, crying.
Tiny little fingers gripped Mihai’s finger tightly.
His colleague asked him: “Daddy, would you like to hold her?” With trembling hands, Mihai held his daughter for the first time.
“Three thousand two hundred grams. She’s so light, and yet so heavy.” Ana understood very well what he meant.
After a while, Elena and Carmen came into the room.
Elena gently touched her little cheek and spoke the name for the first time: “Rosa Elena.”
Carmen laughed: “She was supposed to be born earlier, and yet she came on time. Not like Ana: this one’s an easy-going soul.”
Elena whispered in Mihai’s ear: “Of the twelve wishes from the New Year’s Eve grapes, the first has already come true.”
Mihai laughed: “Maybe it’s thanks to last night’s ramen. If I tell Kenji, he’ll surely be delighted.”
In Ana’s bag were the pink socks from Sakura. When they put them on her, one was a little bigger and was loose on her.
“So like Sakura. But soon they should fit perfectly.”
At half past seven it began to get light outside. Above the snowy rooftops, the sun rose.
The light came into the room and lit up Rosa Elena’s face.
“A rose that blooms in the light…” Ana said softly. It was the meaning of the name chosen on New Year’s Eve.
With her daughter in her arms, Ana remembered this year: the wedding in Madrid, the honeymoon in the village, the move to Bucharest.
“A year ago it never even crossed my mind that I’d be here.”
Shortly before eight, Elena and Carmen went home for a while to get a little rest. “I’ll help myself to a bit of the ramen in the freezer,” said Carmen.
Mihai called the village. Grandpa was silent for a long time, then said: “A great-granddaughter… Ileana, did you hear?”
“When summer comes, I’ll make her a little stool. Just like yours.”
At eight, Mihai sent the photo to everyone in Japan. The replies came one after another.
At nine, Sakura video-called, having just come home from school.
When the baby appeared on the screen, Sakura shouted “Hana-chan!” and burst into tears.
Behind her, Haruka laughed: “See? I told you she was bound to wait until the due date.”
Around noon, Dr Ionescu came into the room with flowers, just as he was, in his white coat.
He said “Congratulations!” in Japanese and bowed deeply. They were words Mihai had taught him long before.
Then he laughed and said in Romanian: “You’re on leave, and yet you ended up at the hospital anyway.”
Kenji only noticed his phone at seven. He leapt out of bed and ran to the hospital, wearing Mrs Doina’s scarf and Mr Petre’s hat.
But by the rules, visiting hours only started at two. Kenji waited in the lobby the whole time and drank five coffees.
At exactly two o’clock, Kenji quietly opened the door of the room.
All that day, the laughter in the room never stopped.
That evening, Ana wrote just one line in her Japanese diary: “15 January, clear skies. Rosa Elena was born.”

Reading text: Sakura’s letter to Hana-chan
In the evening, Haruka sends a photo of the letter Sakura (9) wrote to the baby, in big round letters.
Hana-chan, thank you for being born. I’m Sakura. Your big sister, who lives in Hiroshima.
I’m the one who gave you the name “Hana-chan”. Rosa and Sakura are both flowers, so we’re flower sisters.
For you, I practise the lullaby on the piano every day. But I heard big brother sang it first. That’s not fair!
